Chapter 4: Building New Habits Through Deliberate Self-Talk.
Habits are really the foundation of our everyday lives. Think about it—so much of what you do, from the moment you wake up to the time you go to bed, is driven by habits. They shape your routines, influence the choices you make, and, over time, they can completely change the direction of your life.
The interesting part? Most habits happen almost automatically, guided by old beliefs and expectations that are tucked away in your subconscious. And here’s where self-talk comes in. The way you talk to yourself acts like a script, quietly nudging your actions one way or another.
If you want to change a habit, you’ve got to start by changing that script. Imagine for a second that your inner voice is constantly saying things like, “I can’t stick to a routine,” or “I always give up.” Sound familiar? It’s no wonder change feels so hard.
So, what’s the first step? Pay attention to that self-talk. Notice what your inner voice is saying, especially when you hit a challenge. Are you making excuses? Are you justifying that old behavior? Getting honest about these patterns is key.
Once you know what the old self-talk sounds like, you can swap it out for something new—something that actually supports the habit you want to build. And it's not about forcing yourself with sheer willpower. Instead, you’re creating a new internal story, one that makes the new behavior feel natural, even inevitable.
Let’s say you want to start exercising more. Rather than repeating, “I always quit,” try telling yourself, “I enjoy taking care of my body,” or “I’m the kind of person who sticks to my commitments.”
Here are a few practical steps to make this shift:
First, write down the habit you want to build. Be as specific as you can.
Next, create a positive, present-tense statement that supports this new habit. Make it personal—something that feels true to you.
Then, repeat that statement every day, especially when you’re most tempted to fall back into the old habit.
Visualize yourself doing the new behavior. Picture it being easy and enjoyable.
And don’t forget to celebrate the small wins. Every little success makes your new self-talk more believable, and that positive emotion helps lock in the change.
This creates a feedback loop. The more you practice the new habit, the stronger your new self-talk becomes. Each success, no matter how small, reinforces your belief. Over time, what once felt hard starts to feel automatic, because your subconscious is now on your side.
Remember, patience matters. Old habits might creep back in—especially when you’re stressed or tired. If that happens, don’t beat yourself up. Just return to your supportive self-talk. Remind yourself, “I’m learning and improving,” or “Every day, I get a little better at this.”
And here’s something powerful—this approach isn’t just for personal goals. You can use deliberate self-talk to improve your relationships, boost your performance at work, take better care of your health… really, any area of life where you want to grow.
So, what’s the real takeaway? The habits you build are shaped by the stories you tell yourself. When you rewrite those stories with purpose and care, you open the door to new patterns—ones that can actually support the life and values you truly want.
